transcript.text: We replaced our old condenser dryer with a heat pump one about a month ago and honestly it's driving me mad, a normal load of towels takes nearly 3 and a half hours, the old one did it in about 90 minutes. It also feels barely warm for the first half hour when I open the door to check. Surely that's not right? Is it faulty?

It is not necessarily faulty, as heat pump dryers are significantly slower than condenser models and typically take longer to dry heavy items like towels. The "barely warm" feeling in the first half hour is normal for this technology as it builds up heat gradually over a long cycle. From what you have described, the most likely cause is clean the lint filter and the condenser/heat exchanger. Can you tell me whether filters/condenser not cleaned recently?

Well I clean the fluff filters after every single load, and I cleaned the other filter (the condenser one I think) about two weeks ago and it looks clean. So no, they're not neglected. I do keep opening the door to check on it though, does that matter?

Yes, opening the door lets heat escape and stops the drying cycle from working efficiently. This significantly increases drying times and uses more energy. From what you have described, the most likely cause is refrigerant / heat-pump circuit (heat-pump). Overloading, or putting clothes in that weren't spun well in the washer, makes drying much slower. The drum should be no more than about two-thirds full. Was it overloaded or were the clothes very wet going in (and have you changed that), or was it a normal, well-spun load?
It's a full load of towels each time, so probably pretty full I suppose. The washer spins them at 1000 rpm. I use the Cotton Cupboard Dry programme. Is that too much?

Yes, the Cotton Cupboard Dry programme is designed for a very dry finish and will take significantly longer than standard cycles. It is normal for this setting to run for several hours to ensure towels are completely dry. From what you have described, the most likely cause is confirm the complaint is genuine failure, not normal heat-pump behaviour. Is it genuinely cold and never drying, or does it dry but just feels cooler / slower than your old dryer?
It does dry them, they come out fully dry at the end, it's just really slow. It's only lukewarm at the start and the drum is just warm, not scorching, after an hour. Is that normal?

Yes, it is normal for a heat pump tumble dryer to take significantly longer than a condenser model. Heat pumps operate at lower temperatures and are designed to be more energy-efficient, which results in longer drying times. From what you have described, the most likely cause is refrigerant / heat-pump circuit (heat-pump). Check the vent hose out of the back: it should be short, without kinks or squashed sections, and clear of fluff all the way to the outside vent. Was it kinked, squashed or blocked (and is it sorted), or was it already clear?

I'm not sure about the vent hose, I don't know what it looks like at the back. Is that something a heat pump dryer even has? Also should I mention it's in my unheated garage, about 8-10 C at the moment?

Yes, all condenser and heat pump tumble dryers have a vent hose or exhaust pipe to release the extracted moisture. You should check the back of your machine for this connection to ensure it is not blocked or kinked. Sensor dryers stop when two metal strips inside the drum (near the filter) feel the laundry is dry. Fabric conditioner can coat them so it stops too early — wipe them with a damp cloth and a little vinegar. Were they coated or dirty (and are they clean now), or were they already clean?

I haven't looked at any metal strips, I wouldn't know where to find them to be honest. And it does dry everything fully at the end, it doesn't stop early. I still haven't looked at the back for a hose either. Does the cold garage make any difference?

Yes, a cold garage significantly impacts performance because heat pump dryers extract warmth from the surrounding air to operate efficiently. At 8-10°C, the unit has less ambient heat to work with, which extends drying times and results in lower initial temperatures. Behind the flap at the bottom front there's a condenser unit (or a second filter on heat-pump models). Take it out and rinse the fluff off under the tap, then let it drip-dry and refit it. Was it clogged with fluff (and is it clean now), or was it already clean?
I cleaned that one two weeks ago and it looked clean, so I think it's fine. It does collect loads of water each cycle though. Is there anything else I should be trying?

Since your dryer is in an unheated garage, the low ambient temperature (8-10°C) significantly reduces efficiency and extends drying times. You should ensure the unit has adequate airflow around it and consider moving it to a warmer room if possible. A short timed programme, "iron dry" or a low dryness level can leave laundry damp. Was a short or low-dryness programme set (and have you changed it), or was it a normal full drying programme?
No, it's the Cotton Cupboard Dry on a full programme, nothing short or low. I can't really move it indoors either, it has to stay in the garage. Is it just going to be slow then?

[Heading: Likely cause: refrigerant / heat-pump circuit (heat-pump)]
Yes, drying times will naturally increase in an unheated garage because heat pump dryers rely on ambient air temperature to function efficiently. Since the room is only 8-10°C, the machine must work harder and longer to extract moisture compared to a warmer environment. From what you have checked, this points to the refrigerant / heat-pump circuit (heat-pump). To find the right part, could you give me the make and model number? It is usually on a sticker inside the door opening.
